# Introduction {#sec-article-01-introduction}

Air quality management in mining municipalities requires information about both the location of emissions and the places affected by them. A source situated in one administrative zone can influence several neighbouring zones, while an extensive polygon can contain a concentrated activity and a large area with a different land-use pattern. Consequently, a zone-wide label can be convenient for public administration yet conceal the internal structure relevant to emission control. In Congonhas, mining, industrial processing, transportation and urban occupation create a setting in which this distinction directly affects the interpretation of territorial priorities.

Spatial planning provides a practical destination for air quality information. Badach et al. (2020) connect air quality management zones with planning applications, supporting a framework in which environmental evidence informs territorial decisions. However, the spatial support of the evidence needs to be distinguished from the legal unit receiving the information. The present study retains municipal zoning as the management reference while examining concentration patterns before administrative aggregation.

Empirical regionalization and affinity-zone delineation offer complementary ways to describe these patterns (Vienneau and Briggs, 2013). Liu et al. (2018) delineated PM~2.5~ interaction regions using temporal similarity and spatial construction. Akhtar and Han (2026) used hierarchical clustering to redefine air quality zones from pollution behaviour. These studies support testing data-derived boundaries, but their prediction improvements cannot be transferred to the present model scenario. Here, unsupervised clustering is used to examine the structure of existing simulated concentrations and to compare the information provided by alternative classifications.

Relative classification also needs a spatial reliability assessment. Quintiles rank locations within a domain, whereas local indicators of spatial association evaluate a location in relation to its neighbours (Anselin, 1995). A high concentration can therefore belong to a high–high cluster, be spatially isolated, or remain statistically unresolved. None of these labels establishes legal attainment. Moreover, spatial dependence complicates evaluation of emission–concentration relationships, motivating validation procedures that retain spatial structure (Roberts et al., 2017).

We investigate whether receptor-based spatial analyses reveal management-relevant differences that are obscured by broad attainment-oriented classifications, and how those differences change with neighbourhood and aggregation choices. The contribution is an auditable connection between model-derived patterns, source groups and municipal zoning, accompanied by explicit tests of spatial support. The study does not assume that regionalization removes errors in emissions, meteorology or concentration prediction.
